title: Stack vs Heap Allocation
summary: Every value at runtime lives in one of two places. The stack is fast and automatic; the heap is flexible and expensive. Every later topic in this group is a story about who manages the heap.

slides.markdown:
Every variable you write has to live somewhere in memory while your program runs. There are exactly two places: the **stack**, a strict LIFO region tied to function calls, and the **heap**, a general pool for anything that needs to outlive the call that created it.

The stack is basically free — allocation is a pointer bump, deallocation is popping a frame. The heap costs real work: finding free space, tracking what's live, and eventually deciding when to reclaim it. That reclamation question is the seed of everything else in this group — manual `free`, reference counting, tracing GC, and Rust's ownership model are all different answers to "who frees heap memory, and when."

Get this model solid first: it's the vocabulary every later topic assumes.

slides.sectionTitle: The stack: frames in, frames out
slides.subTitle: LIFO by construction
slides.markdown:
Every function call pushes a **stack frame**: space for its local variables, its parameters, and the return address. When the function returns, that whole frame is popped in one shot.

This works because call order is inherently last-in-first-out — the most recently called function is always the next to return. There's no bookkeeping needed: the stack pointer just moves down on a call and back up on a return.

A local `int x = 5` inside a function lives inside that function's frame. The instant the function returns, `x` is gone — not zeroed, not marked, just no longer addressable because the frame above it has been reclaimed.

slides.sectionTitle: The heap: anything that outlives the call
slides.markdown:
The heap exists for exactly the case the stack can't handle: a value that needs to survive after the function that created it returns, or whose size isn't known until runtime.

A node you're inserting into a linked list, a buffer you're filling from a network socket, an object you're about to return by reference — all of these need a lifetime independent of any one call frame. That's a **heap allocation**: carved out of a large, unordered pool, addressable by pointer, and returned to the pool on some separate, explicit decision.

That "separate, explicit decision" is the hard part. The stack answers "when is this freed?" automatically — frame pop. The heap doesn't answer it at all; something else has to.

The stack and heap sit in the same address space but grow in opposite directions and behave nothing alike.

![A process address space with a growing and shrinking call stack above a heap of scattered allocated blocks](assets/stack-heap-address-space.svg)

The arrow in that picture is the important detail: a stack frame routinely holds a **pointer into the heap**. The pointer itself is stack-allocated and dies with the frame; the object it points to does not, unless something else frees it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the stack is nearly free
slides.subTitle: Pointer-bump vs bookkeeping
slides.markdown:
Stack allocation is one instruction: decrement the stack pointer by the frame size. Deallocation is the same instruction in reverse. No search, no metadata, no risk of two frames overlapping — the compiler computed the frame's exact size at compile time.

Heap allocation has none of those guarantees. `malloc` has to find a free block of the right size (a free list walk or a size-class lookup), record how big the block is so `free` later knows how much to reclaim, and possibly split or merge blocks to avoid fragmentation. All of that is real CPU work — commonly 10-100x the cost of a stack push, and that gap is *before* counting cache effects from jumping around a heap versus staying on one contiguous, cache-hot stack page.

This cost difference is why "can this go on the stack instead" is a real performance question, not a style preference.

slides.sectionTitle: Escape analysis: letting the compiler decide
slides.markdown:
Every heap-allocated value in your source doesn't have to become a heap allocation in the compiled program. Modern compilers run **escape analysis**: prove that a value never outlives the function that creates it — never gets returned, stored in a global, or captured by something that survives — and promote it to the stack instead.

Go does this aggressively: `x := &Point{1, 2}` looks like a heap pointer, but if `x` never escapes the function, the compiler stack-allocates the `Point` and the whole thing is as cheap as a local variable. The JVM's JIT does the same for objects it can prove are call-local, skipping allocation and GC pressure entirely.

This is why "heap objects are always slow" is an overstatement in modern runtimes — the source-level allocation site doesn't fully determine the runtime allocation. It's still true for languages without this analysis (plain C, unoptimized code), which is why the mental model still matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Returning a pointer into a popped frame
Who exposes the choice, who hides it
slides.markdown:
| Language | Stack/heap choice | Who decides |
|---|---|---|
| C | Explicit — `int x` vs `malloc()` | You, every time |
| C++ | Explicit, plus RAII to automate heap cleanup | You choose placement, destructors handle freeing |
| Rust | Explicit placement, but the borrow checker verifies lifetimes | You, checked at compile time |
| Java / Python | Hidden — every object is conceptually heap, primitives may be stack | The runtime and JIT |

C and C++ make you name where a value lives. Java and Python collapse the distinction from the programmer's point of view: `new Point()` always reads as a heap allocation in the source, even though the JIT may quietly stack-allocate it underneath via escape analysis (previous slide). Knowing which category your language falls into tells you how much of this topic is your problem versus the runtime's.

slides.sectionTitle: The stack has a limit, and it's small
slides.markdown:
Stack space is fixed at thread creation — typically **1-8 MB** on a modern OS thread, far smaller than available heap. Every recursive call adds a frame, and a recursion that's too deep or has too little work done per call to justify iteration will exhaust it: a **stack overflow**.

A function that recurses on unbounded input without a base case that's actually reachable, or one that builds a large local array on every call, is the classic culprit — 100,000 levels of recursion at even 64 bytes a frame is 6.4 MB, already past a typical default.

The fix is rewriting the recursion as a loop with an explicit heap-allocated stack (a `Vec`/`ArrayList` you manage), or in languages that support it, relying on tail-call elimination so the frame is reused instead of growing. Not all languages guarantee tail-call elimination — don't assume it without checking.

Stack lifetime is free because it's structural — tied to a call that will definitely return. Heap lifetime has no such structure: a heap value's owner, or the point at which it becomes safe to free, has to come from somewhere else.

The rest of this group is that "somewhere else," in order of how automatic it gets: [manual-memory-management](manual-memory-management) hands the decision entirely to the programmer, [reference-counting](reference-counting) and tracing GC automate it at a runtime cost, and [ownership-and-borrowing](ownership-and-borrowing) proves it at compile time instead. Same underlying problem, four different trade-offs between programmer effort, runtime cost, and safety.
